## Batch job examples with TrimGalore

In the [week 6 assignment](../week06/w6_ga.qmd),
you wrote a script to run TrimGalore,
and eventually ran that script for all samples using a loop.
However, this took a while to run -- and consider that these FASTQ files were
subsamples and ~20x smaller than the original (and than typical) FASTQ files.
As such, it would take many hours for that loop to finish on full-size files.

Given that we have access to OSC,
the best way to speed things up in such cases is by submitting a batch job for
each sample.
In most cases^[But keep in mind that batch jobs can be queued/waiting for a while,
especially if you submit large amounts of jobs.],
these jobs will then all run simultaneously (in parallel).

Let's practice running the TrimGalore script using batch jobs.
We'll start with submitting one for a single sample,
and then we'll loop over all samples.
First, get a copy of that script:

```bash
cp ../week06/assignment/scripts/trimgalore.sh scripts/
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### ...Or download a version of this script if you don't have it _(Click to expand)_
```bash
wget -P scripts <TBA-URL>
```
:::

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

#### Modifying the script for usage with Slurm

Next, add Slurm options with the following `#SBATCH` lines in the script ---
note that you'll be asking for 8 cores:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=PAS2880
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mail-type=FAIL
#SBATCH --name=slurm-trimgalore-%j.out
```

When you have multiple cores at your disposal in a job,
you will almost always want to **explicitly tell the program you're running about this**.
Some programs default to using 1 core while others try to auto-detect the number of cores,
but any auto-detection tends to be inappropriate:
the program would detect the total number of cores on the OSC node rather than the
number that we have reserved.
Let TrimGalore know how many cores you have reserved by _editing the command_
to include `--cores 8`:

```bash
# [Other TrimGalore options not shows - same as before]
trim_galore \
    --cores 8 \
```

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

#### Submitting the script as a batch job

Now, you're ready to submit the script. Let's test it for _one sample_ first:

```bash
R1=garrigos-data/fastq/ERR10802863_R1.fastq.gz
R2=${R1/_R1/_R2}
sbatch scripts/trimgalore.sh "$R1" "$R2" results/trimgalore
```
```bash-out
submitted batch job TBA
```

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

#### Monitoring the batch job

Next, monitor your job by:

- Checking its status in the Slurm queue with `squeue -u $USER`
- Checking the contents of the Slurm log file that should appear in your working dir

```bash
squeue -u $USER -l
```
```bash-out
TBA
```

After a while:

- You will know that your job is no longer running
  (either due to failure or because it finished succesfully)
  when it is no longer listed in the `squeue` output
- If you _additionally_ didn't receive an email from Slurm
  (you should have gotten one if the job failed due to the `#SBATCH --mail-type=FAIL` line),
  this implies that it succeeded.

But don't forget to look at the output files:

- **Slurm log file**: Because of our Strict bash `set` settings and an `echo` line
  at the end of the script,
  the presence of the marker line "_Succesfully finished [...]_" means that the
  script encountered no errors.
  That said, you'll always want to also look at the rest of the contents of this
  file, as a program's "logging statements" may have useful information,
  including output summaries but also warnings.
- **Program output files**: Most bioinformatics tools don't just print logging
  information, which end up in the Slurm log file, but will also have output files.
  In the case of TrimGalore, the main output are processed (trimmed) FASTQ files.
  Therefore, always check the output dir for the presence of output files
  
```bash
ls
```
```bash-out
slurm-trimgalore-TBA.out
```

```bash
tail slurm-trimgalore-TBA.out
```
```bash-out
TBA
```

```bash
less slurm-trimgalore*
```

```bash
ls -lh results/trimgalore
```
```bash-out
TBA
```

Because this was a test-run and we'll now run the loop for each sample,
we'll remove all outputs:

```bash
rm -r results/trimgalore slurm-trimgalore*
```

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

#### Submitting a job for each sample

Now, loop over all R1 files to submit a job for each sample: 

```bash
for R1 in garrigos-data/fastq/*_R1.fastq.gz; do
    R2=${R1/_R1/_R2}
    sbatch scripts/trimgalore.sh "$R1" "$R2" results/trimgalore
done
```
```bash-out
submitted batch job TBA
submitted batch job TBA
submitted batch job TBA
submitted batch job TBA
# [...output truncated...]
```

As you saw, all these jobs were submitted in very quick succession, ...

Check the queue:

```bash
squeue -u $USER
```

Once all jobs have finished (are no longer in the queue), let's:

- Take a close look at one Slurm log file:

  ```bash
  less slurm-trimgalore-*
  ```

- Check the last few lines of all of them:

  ```bash
  tail slurm-trimgalore-*
  ```

If everything looks good, and we consider the jobs to have succesfully finished,
all that is left is to clean up the Slurm log files.
In this case, it makes sense to **keep these files**,
as they will contain information ... TBA.

But we do want to move them out of the working dir.
It often makes sense to store them in a subdir of the program's outdir, e.g.:

```bash
mkdir results/trimgalore/logs
mv slurm-trimgalore-* logs/
```

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: callout-tip
#### See output added to the Slurm log file in real time
Text will be added to the Slurm log file in real time as the running script
(or the program ran by the script) outputs it.
However, the output that commands like `cat` and `less` print are static.

Therefore, if you find yourself opening/printing the contents of the Slurm log
file again and again to keep track of progress,
then instead **use `tail -f`**, which will "follow" the file and _will_ print new
text as it's added to the Slurm log file:

```bash
# See the last lines of the file, with new contents added in real time
tail -f slurm-12520046.out
```

To exit the `tail -f` livestream, press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd>.
:::

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

### Recap: Making sure your jobs ran successfully

To recap, here is an overview of basic strategies to monitor your batch jobs:

- To see whether your job(s) have started,
  check the queue (with `squeue`) or check for the appearance of Slurm log files
  (with `ls`).
  
- Once the jobs are no longer listed in the queue,
  they will have finished: either successfully or because of an error.

- When you've submitted many jobs that run the same script for different samples/files:
  - For at least 1 one of the jobs,
    carefully read the full Slurm log file, and check other output files,
  - Check whether no jobs have failed: via email when using `--mail-type=END`,
    or by checking the `tail` of each log for messages like
    "Successfully finished script".
  - Check that you have the expected number of output files and that no files
    have size zero (run `ls -lh`).

## "Protocol" Markdown files

In the past few weeks of this course,
you've created Markdown files with the commands you used to run your scripts.
These files were useful to type and store that code:
alternatively, you could directly type this in the terminal,
but this would be harder to get right (e.g., with loops)
and most importantly would reduce reproducibility,
since you wouldn't have a good record of what you did.

However, these files have so far been very short,
and may not have given you much of a picture of how this would look in the context
of a research project that would include running a whole series of steps
with different bioinformatics tools (and perhaps custom scripts).
For **larger projects**,
you will probably want to create at least two separate Markdown files that contain
the code you used to run scripts and other commands:

- A "lab notebook"-style file that has chronological entries with everything of note
  that you did, including mishaps, dead ends, and things that were redone differently
  later on.

- A "protocol" (or "recipe" / "workflow")-style file that has the final code in
  the order needed to run and rerun your entire project's computational work.

### An RNA-Seq example

While thinking about ways to organize and run your analyses,
let's have an example in mind with a simple RNA-Seq analysis that:

- Trims reads in FASTQ files _(independently for each sample)_
- Maps (aligns) reads to a reference genome _(independently for each sample)_
- Creates a gene expression count table from the alignments _(for all samples together)_

![A simple 3-step RNA-Seq analysis, with arrows showing the connections<br>between the steps: the output of one step is the input of the next.<br>The example only has 3 samples, and the first two steps are executed separately<br>for each sample, while the last step is executed once for all samples.](../img/schem-workflow.svg){fig-align="center" width="70%" fig-alt="A diagram of the steps in a simple RNA-Seq analysis." .lightbox}

Here is an example "protocol-style" Markdown file for this RNA-seq analysis:

````markdown

## Set up: Define the input files

```bash
# [hypothetical example - don't run any of the code in this document]
fastq_dir=data/fastq
ref_assembly=data/ref/assembly.fna
ref_annotation=data/ref/annotation.gtf
```

## Step 1: Trim the reads

The `map.sh` script takes 3 arguments -- R1 FASTQ, ref. assembly, and output dir:

```bash
for R1 in "$fastq_dir"/*_R1.fastq.gz; do
    # (The trim.sh script takes 2 arguments: R1 FASTQ and output dir)
    sbatch scripts/trim.sh "$R1" results/trim
done
```

## Step 2: Align (map) the reads to a reference genome assembly

The `map.sh` script takes 3 arguments -- R1 FASTQ, ref. assembly, and output dir:

```bash
for R1 in results/trim/*_R1.fastq.gz; do
    sbatch scripts/map.sh "$R1" "$ref_assembly" results/map
done
```

## Step 3: Count alignments per sample per gene using the annotation:

The `count.sh` script takes 3 arguments -- input dir, ref. annotation, and output dir:

```bash
sbatch scripts/count.sh results/map "$ref_annotation" results/count_table.txt
```
````

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

### The rationale behind organizing and running scripts this way

The protocol above runs a primary shell script for each of the three steps
(`trim.sh`, `map.sh`, and` count.sh`),
and each of these _takes arguments_ and runs a bioinformatics tool to perform
that step (for example, TrimGalore for trimming).

Here are some advantages of using such a script structure with flexible
(i.e., argument-accepting) scripts,
and an overarching protocol Markdown file to describe the entire workflow:

- Rerunning everything, including with a modified sample set, or tool settings,
  is relatively straightforward --- both for yourself and others, improving reproducibility.
- Re-applying the same set of analyses in a different project is straightforward.
- The Markdown file documents the steps taken.
- It (more or less) ensures you are including all necessary steps.

::: callout-tip
### Why use variables

Above, we saw that variables are useful to be able to **pass arguments to a script**,
so you can easily rerun a script with a different input file / settings / etc.
Let's take a step back and think about variables and their uses once again.

> *"Processing pipelines having numerous settings that should be stored in variables
(e.g., which directories to store results in, parameter values for commands,
input files, etc.).*\
>*Storing these settings in a variable defined at the top of the file makes adjusting
settings and rerunning your pipelines much easier.*\
>*Rather than having to change
numerous hardcoded values in your scripts, using variables to store settings means
you only have to change one value—the value you’ve assigned to the variable."*  

@buffalo2015 - Chapter 12

In brief, recall that variables are especially useful for things that
you refer to repeatedly and/or are subject to change.
:::

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

## Pipelines

What exactly do we mean by a "pipeline"?
We may informally refer to any consecutive series of analysis steps as a pipeline.
The above Markdown document, in particular, can informally be called a pipeline.
But here, I am using pipeline in a stricter sense to mean a series of steps that
**can be executed from start to finish with a single command**.

An advantage of a true pipeline is increased automation,
as well as "supercharging" the above-mentioned advantages of the discussed script structure.
For example, a pipeline _truly_ ensures that you are including all necessary steps.

### Why the above Markdown file is not a true pipeline

The above Markdown file is intentionally set up to run the bits of code block-by-block
rather than all at once.

This is because you're not able to run all the code at once in its current form.
There are multiple batch job steps where the input of a later step uses the output
of an earlier step.
Therefore, if you run all code at once,
all batch jobs will be submitted at the same time,
and later steps will start running before the earlier step has finished.

For example, consider the following two consecutive steps,
in which the second step uses the output of the first step: 

```bash
# This script creates a genome "index" for STAR, that will be used in the next step
# ('my_genome.fa' = input genome FASTA, 'results/star_index' = output index dir)
sbatch scripts/star_index.sh my_genome.fa results/star_index

# This script aligns a FASTQ file to the genome index created in the previous step
# ('results/star_index' = input index dir, 'sampleA.fastq.gz' = input FASTQ file,
# 'results/star_align' = output dir)
sbatch scripts/star_align.sh results/star_index sampleA.fastq.gz results/star_align 
```

If these two lines were included in your runner script,
and you would run that script in its entirety all at once,
the script in the second step would be submitted just a split-second after the
first one
(when using `sbatch`, you get your prompt back immediately -- there is no waiting).
As such, it would fail because of the missing output from the first step.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

### What can we do, then?

Having to wait for each step to finish before submitting the next step is a bit
tedious. How could you automate this and create a true pipeline?

Foremost, you'd need to overcome the problem of simultaneous batch job submission.
But a decent pipeline **detect failure and then stop**,
and to **rerun parts of the pipeline** flexibly.
The latter may be necessary after, e.g.:
  
- Some scripts failed for all or some samples
- You added or removed a sample
- You had to modify a script or settings somewhere halfway the pipeline.

How could you implement all of that?

- **Push the limits of the Bash and Slurm tool set (not recommended)**\
  Use `if` statements, additional script arguments, and Slurm "job dependencies"
  (see the [optional reading page](../bonus/slurm.html)) ---
  but this is hard to manage for more complex workflows.

- **Use a formal workflow management system (recommended)**\
  Workflow management systems like
  [Snakemake](https://snakemake.readthedocs.io/) or
  [NextFlow](https://www.nextflow.io/)
  can take care of all these details and more for you ---
  we will talk about Nextflow later in this course!

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
#### How about writing multi-step scripts? 

Once you get the hang of writing shell scripts,
it may also seem appealing to string a series of programs/steps together in a single script.

At the extreme, you could solve the simultaneous batch job problem by putting all
steps in a single script,
but this would make for a very inefficient pipeline,
since you'd now be running steps that can be parallelized across samples consecutively^[
Unless you'd try to hack your way around that, but at that point you run into
the same problems as mentioned above under "Push the limits of...".
].

A bit more reasonably,
you could add multiple consecutive per-sample steps in a single script.
E.g. a script that would trim and then align reads for a single sample.
This would reduce the number of times you have to submit scripts and wait for the
results before moving on.
In practice, though, this will often end up leading to more difficulties than convenience.

All in all,
It is a good idea to keep your shell scripts simple
_in the sense that they should generally **just run one program**_,
and not a sequence of programs.
:::
